displayQuote: Don't look back. Something might be gaining on you

meta.title: Who really said "Don't look back. Something might be gaining on you"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Yes — Satchel Paige, the last of six rules for staying young, printed in Collier’s on 13 June 1953. The wording started drifting within months.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Don't look back. Something might be gaining on you'?
meta.ogDescription: The last of Paige’s six rules for staying young, in Collier’s, June 1953. Verified — and drifting ever since.

answer.label: Spoken by

answer.sourceLine: The last of six rules Paige gave under the heading “How to Stay Young,” printed in a sidebar to Richard Donovan’s profile of him in Collier’s, dated 13 June 1953. Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes the sidebar and gives the quote page as 55.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “Time Ain’t Gonna Mess with Me” by Richard Donovan
A sidebar of six quotations headed “How to Stay Young”

source.excerpt: If your stomach disputes you, lie down and pacify it with cool thoughts. … Go very light on the vices, such as carrying on in society. The social ramble ain’t restful. … Don’t look back. Something might be gaining on you.
trail: Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes the sidebar from Collier’s of 13 June 1953 and concludes: “Satchel Paige deserves credit for this quotation which appeared in the sidebar of a 1953 Collier’s magazine article.”

The same page shows the line in print before the cover date: an advertisement for the issue ran in New York’s Daily News on 5 June 1953, promising “Satch’s own six rules for longevity” and quoting this one as the ending.
Wikiquote ↗ independently cites “How to Stay Young,” Collier’s Magazine (13 June 1953) for the same rule.

Quote Investigator further records that both The Quote Verifier (Ralph Keyes, 2006, p. 133) and The Yale Book of Quotations (Fred R. Shapiro, 2006, p. 575) carry the saying with a Collier’s citation. We have not handled either book; those locators are Quote Investigator’s.
source.excerptNote: Three of the six as Quote Investigator ↗ transcribes them. Wikiquote ↗ prints a fuller run of the list, with “Avoid running at all times” immediately before the last rule.
source.rightsHolder: The Crowell-Collier Publishing Company (Collier’s) and the estate of Leroy Paige
source.rightsNote: The sidebar appeared in Collier’s dated 13 June 1953. The United States public domain currently reaches published works from before 1931, so a 1953 magazine is in copyright. Quote the line with attribution rather than reprinting the article.

author.name: Satchel Paige
author.heading: About Satchel Paige
author.metaLine: 1906–1982 · Negro leagues and Major League pitcher
author.bio: Leroy Robert “Satchel” Paige began pitching in the Negro leagues with the Birmingham Black Barons in 1927 and did not reach the Major Leagues until 9 July 1948, when he debuted for the Cleveland Indians at 42. That season he became the first player who had played in the Negro leagues to pitch in a World Series. He threw his last Major League game for the Kansas City Athletics in September 1965, two weeks shy of 60, and in 1971 became the first player elected by the Hall of Fame’s Negro League Committee.

misattribution.heading: Often misquoted
misattribution.intro: The attribution is not in doubt. The wording is. Paige’s sixth rule began drifting within months of publication and is still quoted in forms he did not use.

items.who: “Don’t look back — somebody may be gaining on you”
items.why: In November 1953 an Allentown, Pennsylvania paper reported Associated Press sports editor Orlo Robertson giving the rule this way: “something might” had already become “somebody may.” Quote Investigator ↗
A syndicated columnist in The Atlanta Constitution of 8 June 1955 printed it with “someone” in place of “something.”

items.who: “Never look back. You might see someone overtaking you!”
items.why: A columnist in an Auburn, California paper printed this version in June 1960 with no credit to Paige at all.
Profiled in The Miami Herald in 1987, the producer quoted it as “don’t look back, somebody will be following you” — credited to Paige, but not what Paige said.

misattribution.truthLine: The wording Collier’s printed on 13 June 1953 is the one above, and it is Paige’s. Quote Investigator ↗ concludes that he “deserves credit for this quotation.”

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Paige was pitching in the Major Leagues in his late forties when Collier’s ran this, and the magazine knew exactly what it had. Its own advertisement, out on 5 June 1953, led with the question: “How has Satchel Paige managed to outlast the great DiMaggio and so many others who began their careers long after he was an established star?”

The six rules answer it as a joke that is not quite a joke. Five are about the body — fried meats, the stomach, the social ramble. The sixth is about the mind, and it is the one that outlived the other five, because it stopped being advice about ageing and became advice about everything.
detailsBody: The rules were printed as a sidebar to “Time Ain’t Gonna Mess with Me,” the concluding part of Richard Donovan’s profile “The Fabulous Satchel Paige,” starting on page 54 of the 13 June 1953 Collier’s, with this quotation on page 55.

Quote Investigator notes an older current the rule swims in: the warning against looking back is the story of Lot’s wife, and a 1907 Kansas valedictorian had already told a graduating class that those who stop to look back get overtaken. Paige did not need either. What he added was the menace of leaving the thing behind you unnamed.

sourcesVerified.claim: Quote Investigator transcribes this exact wording from the "How to Stay Young" sidebar in Collier’s of 13 June 1953 (article by Richard Donovan, quote page 55) and concludes Paige deserves credit for it.
Quote Investigator documents the 5 June 1953 Daily News advertisement quoting the rule before the cover date, and the 1953, 1955, 1960 and 1987 variant wordings.
Wikiquote cites "How to Stay Young," Collier’s Magazine (13 June 1953) for this rule.
Wikipedia gives Paige’s birth date as July 7, 1906, making him 46 at the time of the June 1953 issue.
